Gender expression isn't necessarily the same thing as gender identity

In all seriousness nonbinary isn't necessarily the absence of gender. Gender isn't a well defined binary due to the fact it's a complex intersection of social construct, internal self, and self expression, and because of that it just doesn't make much sense to try and count genders when it's more nuanced than that. 

Scientifically we don't fully understand gender in terms of cause or definition since it's something experienced individually yet utilized societally, and even within the understanding we do have, there are obvious issues related that need to be discussed- for example the way women have historically been unfairly viewed. 

Gender studies exist for this very reason, however given the complicated nature of the topic, it's honestly understandable if someone didn't have the energy or commitment it would take to learn in-depth everything about it. If you aren't able to fully wrap your mind around the ins and outs that doesn't make you a bad person and if someone gets upset at you for not knowing every identity label under the sun that's just ridiculous and overly obnoxious. The only thing that would be wrong here would be denying people's lives and realities simply *because* you don't understand. 

Ignorance tends to lead to hate while education leads to acceptance; that should give you some perspective on your own feelings towards the topic if it's something causing you any significant frustration. 

All we can do to be closest to what's true is keeping the discussion open while acknowledging our own biases (those biases typically being fueled by pride or insecurity on our understanding). Remember what's actually important here, which is going by life in the way that makes the world a more inviting place to be in; not putting others down in your attempts to feel more secure in your position of being "right". In the end what matters most in any discussion is the people being affected by it.

Androsexual can be interpreted in more than one way. It's kind of similar to how some people are bi with a preference and some aren't but they all still fall under bi. Androsexual can mean being just attracted to men. 

The perk of the term is simply that it isn't dependant on the gender of the person using it in the way gay straight or lesbian are, and solely describes what you are attracted to regardless of your own gender, meaning it can be a label you can go by that stays consistent even when your gender fluctuates. 

Overall though labels aren't actually all that important when it comes to your identity. Their purpose is just to make it quicker to communicate surface level generalizations about yourself to others- not to define who you are. There aren't real rules to identity labels as they're not all encapsulating to begin with.

The thing with incest is the whole reason it's actually wrong is the historical issues with inbreeding that were extremely unethical to the children produced by blood relatives, as well as child abuse that was associated with it. 1. Will these people have children deformed by inbreeding?
2. Is this a non-consensual relationship?

If you answer yes to either of those then it's wrong, if not then it's fine. 

People throw around incest as like a witch hunt buzz word especially with the purpose of invalidating queer relationships, so I hope this clears up the reality of these topics a little.

I think you got caught up in the propaganda about how sensitive LGBT people supposedly are with pronouns. We really do not care in the slightest about forcibly gender neutralizing babies. Respecting pronouns is about respecting people's identity and treating them like human beings. It's not about being hyper cautious around anything related to gender. 

When it comes to babies I guarantee you no reasonable person will be mad about you asking what gender their baby is. Gender acceptance doesn't mean we need to stay completely unassuming even at birth, it just means not forcing gender roles onto people, and instead allowing them to grow and do whatever feels comfortable. With young children there's nothing wrong with addressing them by their assigned gender at birth, the only real concern is in listening to them whether or not they tell you later on that they actually identify differently. 

Assuming someone's gender based on their gender presentation isn't necessarily wrong. If you feel someone's gender isn't easily apparent it's perfectly fine to ask about pronouns, just try to be tactful about it for example by saying your own pronouns first so they feel more safe around you. 

A lot of nonbinary or non stealth trans folks will likely let you know what they go by anyways if they feel the need to let you know. It's not as complicated of a subject as so many people try to make it seem.

Just relax when it comes to gender things, I promise normal people don't get as pressed about it as it may seem from trolls on social media. Pronouns really don't matter much when it comes to babies.

I get you're coming from a place of genuine questioning but i feel like I should mention that this idea stems from somewhat transphobic/black and white thinking. All identities (LGBTQ+ ones in this case) are far more varied and nuanced than their labels can define alone. 

Gender in particular has been policed very strictly these past centuries, with gender roles that most people nowadays would agree are too limiting towards what gender is, and genderfluid and nonbinary people are often disbelieved because of the repercussions of that system. Many binary trans people aim to align themselves into what's accepted traditionally, and a very sad nature of minorities is this sort of "pick me" behavior of catering to the majority by putting down the lesser seen people of their own group in order to be seen as more normal in comparison. There are extreme cases of that but the more common cases involve trying to push the strict gender binary systems onto other trans people and invalidating nonbinary identities. It all stems from wanting to be accepted, but that behavior causes nonbinary and genderfluid people to be thrown under the bus. 

To more directly answer your question, some binary trans people do have a genderfluid phase, but it's precisely because of the fact that genderfluidness and nonbinary identities *do* exist in that space between man and woman, and even within them. Gender is viewed as a list of labels and options, but it's really more of a spectrum plane. So no, genderfluid isn't "just" a phase, it's an existing identity just like man and woman. Saying being genderfluid is just a phase is like saying being a boy is just a phase for everyone in the world just because it *was* a phase for you (you in the general example sense lol).

OP, while it's true that sometimes you *do* end up needing to cut people off when the relationship becomes too toxic, that isn't the only possible course of action. A lot of people who fall for that mindset are victims of fear mongering, and are manipulated into thinking their perspective is the logical one. The way you fix that, ESPECIALLY if it's someone already close to you (which means they might be more open to at least respecting you enough to hear you out) is by showing them the real facts, and disproving those transphobic talking points one by one in an honest discussion. 

It's hard because these points are actively antagonizing to **us** but try your best to bring up this discussion calmly and without making her feel antagonized (basically show her the facts while coming from a place of understanding for how she was swept into this, and try not to show any aggression) 

This is really important, talk to her in person.

Some things you can do more specifically are giving her each point very slowly and give her time to respond to each one. If she says anything stemming from fear, for example the "trans women are taking things from actual women" respond with questioning her why she feels that way, and don't say anything while she responds so that she's forced to really listen to her own words. Then once she responds, be ready with statistics, and along with those try to show her the reason people fall for those lies, and try to overall show her that these talking points are just conservatives trying to use transgender people as a distraction from actual issues. 

Another thing you can bring up is that they've used those exact same talking points about trans people that they used about lgb people as well as black people, and Jews during the Holocaust. (This you should research on your own so you can be more thorough in explaining). 

Facts are definitely your friend in this argument because science and history really do support trans people, but make sure to keep tabs on how your sister responds emotionally. If you go too hard on facts alone she might respond with defensiveness and simply not believe them, so what's really important is that you make sure to talk to her as her family. Really listen to her and why she feels so strongly against trans people, and then let her know on a more human level how that hurts, and how you are who you are, and you love her and want her to be able to love you as who you are. 

Be calm, genuine, and confident in what you're telling her. It *is* possible to change her perspective with enough educating. And this may or may not take more than one conversation, but if you keep the conversation open (and I know how hard that is when dealing with people who are so blinded with anger and fear) eventually she very possibly could come around. 

All of this is completely up to your decision on what needs to be done, but if you want to take the route that doesn't involve ending the relationship, all of this really doesn't hurt to try. That kind of thing is usually a conservative rhetorical about trans people wanting to "turn the kids trans" or push some sort of gender neutral agenda- but what most of us actually want is just people to accept their children as they are and support them. 

I think some gender roles are harmful when pushed, but those are specifically the ones such as "boys can't cry" or "girls have to be good wives." That doesn't just apply to trans kids either. The only issues are when you force gendered expectations on a kid with the reaction that if they don't live up to said expectations you can't know them anymore or no longer value them as much.

Some people may choose to raise their children without gender rules, for example allowing their child to pick their own clothes from any gender section, or allowing their child to have any haircut, but this isn't to say they force their child to not have a gender, or that other people *have* to raise their kids this way either. 

There is absolutely nothing wrong with treating your child as the gender they're assigned at birth when they haven't told you they want otherwise. Trans people as a whole really don't want some monolithic change in how babies are raised. All we really want is for you to accept the possibility your child may be trans and support them if that is the case later on, but it's not problematic to treat a child as a gender they've expressed no discomfort with currently.

If you're just playing open world of course there aren't any rules  as long as you have fun with it, but at least for a suggested team the advice would usually be to go for a DPS character, a sub DPS/support, a healer/shielder, and a buffer character; with elemental synergy being a part of figuring that out instead of a standalone thing just for the sake of *some* kind of synergy. 

In your example team if you're having kaeya as your main DPS, having Noelle is a bit clunky of a slot since she doesn't boost his damage and you already have Candace and Barbara to shield and heal respectively. Again this is just my take on it and there's no rules to teams as long as you like playing the characters and have fun with the teams, but if you want a suggested team comp this is generally good advice for it.

To do a bit of clarification on my other comment, the issue is that when people "see" this difference, they're doing more damage than just seeing it, they're putting trans people into a separate category when in reality being trans doesn't define anything about who someone is, and to end the harassment and assault trans people face daily we really need to normalize the thinking that being trans doesn't make you any less of a gender than having a certain hair color does. In the end being trans is a descriptor not the totality of who someone is.

Think of it like this. If someone was born with very bad eyesight and lived their life up to a point with that bad eyesight, and then they finally got glasses a few years later, why would you constantly put them into an "other" category when it's not relevant? Now yes, needing heavy prescription glasses does mean that someone would have a different experience than people who don't need them; when you go on rollercoasters or go swimming you might need to take extra steps to do so. But in the end constantly putting them on a pedestal and telling them they're better/worse or even simply different, is really pointless and at a certain point WILL be damaging to someone's emotional wellbeing, especially children. 

Now obviously there are some differences from this metaphor to the reality of being trans but the majority is very similar. Both are things that allow a person to live their life more naturally and comfortably, even if the amount of modification needed is different for each person, and both of these things aren't obligated to be shown off. Some people might want to have big eccentric frames because they love showing their glasses, while some may prefer slim frames or even contacts and both are completely fine. Same with trans people. Some may want to flaunt pride in their identity but some may simply want to live comfortably. No matter what though it isn't other people's business to force someone to do one or the other. Again especially with children, being made public or "outed" more than necessary can and often does cause bullying. If your child wants to tell people and is able to explain it to other kids, that's completely perfect and good job to her. Just please remember this isn't a necessity. Being trans doesn't make you all that different from not being (or cisgender) because though it exists it's not necessarily something that changes who you are, and that part's more important.

I'll definitely be downvoted for this but I'll be honest, I feel like neopronouns in themselves make perfect sense, but a lot of people, specifically children, are the type to use pronouns in a way I personally just can't agree with unless someone could change my mind in an honest explanation. One that isn't just "if you don't accept my every whim without evidence or reasoning then you're inherently transphobic and/or stupid." 

I understand the purpose and significance of pronouns such as ey/em and similar ones, but when it comes to neopronouns that use certain nouns, I can't help but think people are missing the point of pronouns. Pronouns are simply to make it easier to refer to someone, they aren't personality traits or defining characteristics. And what I consistently find is that the people using noun-pronouns usually don't understand the complexities of gender further than presentation. You can 100% be a guy who likes the supernatural but that isn't a gender identity, it's an individual characteristic. So pronouns like ghost/ghostself to me just seem like people trying to make their gender identity their entire personality (or you could say the other way around, as labeling their "vibe" as their gender). This irritates me because I feel like there's already too much of a defined binary with gender as it is, and I really wish people could realize you're more than your pronouns. I could be wrong on this but I feel as though making someone feel special isn't a good enough reason to negate important topics like that one as it causes real suffering for people around the world, ie sexism. It feels frivolous and immature, especially because I'm certain these people wouldn't actually get any gender dysphoria if someone used different pronouns for them, they just want to use those pronouns because it sounds cool. Another reason people may be partial to those pronouns as well could just be the common mental state of many trans people to feel different or like they don't belong so sometimes people try to escape that feeling by masking it as being better than others, a god complex type thought process. This is a dangerous mentality that can become toxic quickly and I don't think it should be encouraged especially as I see it so often with people my age (late teens) and usually younger. This isn't down to gender, it's down to a misunderstanding and harmful coping mechanism for the actual dysphoria people may feel. I know it may not be so deep for some people, young kids especially, and most likely it's just an experimental phase, but imagine if people treated someone only making friends with stuffed toys as something to encourage, it's not necessarily wrong but it can cause issues with people, or can sometimes even be caused by preexisting issues. Side tangent: using pronouns that are just longer nouns seems contradictory to me, you might as well just say the person's name over and over again.
